title: Chapter 218 – The Hand That Learned Stone
html:
[Terrace Five – Yue]

Yue wakes with her hand on fire, and the fire is cold.

It is the strangest sensation she has ever known. She lies on the white bench in the honey-colored light with her eyes still closed, and she feels, quite clearly, a burning along the whole length of her left arm, from the shoulder to the tips of the fingers: a bright, bitter, crawling burn, the burn of a limb that has slept too long and is being asked to remember itself. But there is no heat in it. There is no warmth at all. It is the burning of an ice floe in sunlight, the ache of a thing that has forgotten how to be touched.

She opens her eyes.

The tree is over her. It is a squat gnarled thing, with pewter bark and brass leaves, and between the leaves, hanging in clusters like grapes, the amber fruit ticks in the golden air. She has been looking at it for a very long time. She knows, without being told, that she has been looking at it for a year.

Slowly, says a voice.

It is dry and cool and has the flat precision of a blade laid on a table. Yue turns her head. A tall figure in a gray cloak is standing at the foot of the bench, with a hood drawn forward and one bandaged hand held against her breastbone. She does not move. She does not need to. Yue has been told, in the dark of the dream, that this woman has been standing there for a year, and has not once sat down.

"Lady Veyra," she says. Her voice is a croak. She has not used it in a year. "Is it done?"

It is begun. The hood tilts. You have a seed. You have a cost. You have, I should say, a very bad temper, which I take to be a good sign. A pause. Look at your hand.

Yue looks.

She had known what she would see. She had been shown it in the dream, plainly, with the courtesy of a tree that does not like to take without warning. But knowing is not seeing. She lifts the left hand from the bench, slowly, and turns it over in the light.

It is stone.

Not carved. Not gray. It is the color of old honey, the warm pale color of a river pebble, and it is as supple as her own flesh. The fingers bend. The thumb flexes. The knuckles are the knuckles she was born with, and the creases in the palm are the creases she has had since childhood. But under the surface, if she looks closely, the light does not sink in. It lies on the skin like cream on the surface of a bowl. And there is a fine web of dark lines beneath it, as of cracks in a glaze, which run from the wrist to the middle finger and stop.

She flexes the hand.

It does not hurt. It does not feel. She presses her thumb against her forefinger and feels the pressure, the weight, the tension of tendon; but she does not feel the touch. She might be holding a pen. She might be holding nothing at all.

"I can't feel heat," she says.

No.

"I can't feel cold."

You will feel the cold of the Orchard, says Veyra. It is the one cold it permits. But the warmth of a hand, the heat of a fire, the temperature of a cup of tea: these are gone. It is the price for the seed. It is a fair price. A pause. I have seen worse.

Yue closes the hand.

It makes a fist. The knuckles whiten. She feels them, through some distant ghost of proprioception, and does not feel the pain that ought to follow.

"It's my fighting hand," she says, absurdly.

Is it?

"I'm left-handed."

Then you will learn to be right-handed, says Veyra Thann, and the first thing you will find is that it is a great deal less trouble than you expect.

---

She remembers the climb in pieces.

She remembers leaving the Hall at dawn with a pack on her back and a heavy gray cloak around her shoulders, and Mei standing in the great doorway with a white streak in her hair, not weeping, not waving, just standing, with her arms folded and her chin up. She remembers Kuang pressing a roll of oilcloth into her hands. She remembers Tian Mo saying, gruffly, come back, and Hai Ren saying nothing, and a small voice from the shadow of the stair, very thin: Master Yue.

Little Mei had stood on the third step in her nightshirt with her hair in tangles. She had looked at Yue for a long moment with her great dark eyes. Then she had come down the stairs and put something into Yue's palm, a small flat thing, warm from the hand that had held it.

It was a pebble.

For luck, said Little Mei. It's from the courtyard. It's the one I always step on. She had hesitated. You can give it back when you come home.

Yue had put it in her sleeve.

It is there still.

She remembers the Hundred Stairs, white and steep and endless, and the stone Quay at the top, and the long gray plain of the Silent Terrace spread out beneath the cold blue sky. She remembers the great arch with its list of names, and the shed with its lit stove, and the figure beside it. A heavy man in a gray cloak, with his head thrown back and his mouth open on a note that would never end. She remembers standing in front of him for an hour. She remembers Pebble, beside her, weeping without sound.

She remembers the five stone pupils on the lip of the Quay, and the way the nearest one's hand had been open.

She remembers the stair to the Fifth, and the iron post, and the single grain of salt. She remembers picking it up between thumb and forefinger. It had been very small, and very cold, and very bright, and when it vanished from her hand she had felt, quite clearly, something close in her chest, like a door in a house that she would not enter again.

She had not looked back.

She remembers the gate, and the Orchard, and the old woman with the basket who had said, in a voice like wind in a dry field: You are the one who was expected.

By whom? Yue had said.

By a young man who has been sitting under that tree for forty days, said Sorrel, and has not once stopped asking in his sleep for someone called Yue.

She had not wept. She is not a woman who weeps. But she had sat down on the white bench beside him, in the honey-colored light, and taken the fruit that Sorrel offered, and bitten into it with her eyes on his sleeping face. And the dream had come down over her like a lid.

---

The dream is different for everyone, the Keeper told her. It is the tree's last courtesy: a question, and a mirror, and a door.

Hers was a courtyard.

It was a small, bare courtyard, paved with gray slabs, with a single well in the middle and a high wall on all sides. It was the courtyard of the Lin compound in the third week of the war. She knew it at once. She knew the chipped corner of the well-head, the iron ring in the wall where they had tied the horses, the long stain in the flagstones where something had burned. She stood in the center of it in her fighting leathers with her sword on her hip, and nobody else was there.

What are you for? said the tree.

She had not answered at once. She had never been a woman who answered quickly. She had stood in the empty courtyard and looked at the ring in the wall, and thought of every answer she had ever given. To protect the clan. That was one. To hold the gate. That was another. To stand between.

Between what? the tree asked.

Between the thing and the people.

Which thing?

Whichever one comes.

And when it has come?

She had no answer to that.

She stood in the courtyard for a very long time. She watched the shadows move across the stones. At last she said, very quietly, I do not know. It was the truest thing she had ever said. She felt it go out of her like a long breath, and the courtyard shimmered, and the well in the middle began to fill with water.

Look, said the tree.

She looked.

In the black water of the well, small and clear, there was a hand. It was her own hand, the left, the one with the callus on the sword-side of the thumb. It was holding a blade. It had been holding a blade for thirty-one years. The knuckles were scarred, the nails bitten short, and under the skin she could see, as through glass, every cut it had ever taken, every fracture, every healed bone.

This is what you are for, said the tree. Not the blade. The hand.

I don't understand.

A hand holds. It does not choose what it holds. The courtyard grew dim. The question is not what you stand between. It is whether you are willing to stop holding when the thing you hold is no longer yours.

She felt it then: a cold that began at the wrist and moved up, slow and steady and without cruelty, like frost on a window. It was in the fingers. It was in the palm. It was in the bones, the pale small bones she had known all her life, and it was turning them to something harder.

You may keep the blade, said the tree. You may not keep the warmth. Choose.

She had looked at the water for a long time.

I choose the blade, said Yue.

And the courtyard had gone dark.

---

"You're awake."

The voice is rough and tired and very near. She turns her head, slowly, on the bench, and sees a man sitting at the foot of the neighboring tree with his back against the trunk and his knees drawn up. He is thinner than she remembers. There is a thread of white at his temple. He has a steady hand, now, she notices, the left, which he holds loosely in his lap as if he does not quite trust it; and he is looking at her with an expression she has never seen on him.

It is the face of a man who has been waiting for a sentence.

"Jian," she says.

"I'm sorry."

"For what?"

"For all of it." His voice is hoarse. "For the Print. For the ten years. For not telling you first. For leaving. For—" He gestures at the Orchard, at the ticking trees, at the long golden row. "For this."

"You didn't ask me to come."

"No."

"You didn't ask me to stay."

"No."

"Then what are you sorry for?"

He opens his mouth. Closes it.

She sits up. It takes some doing. Her body is stiff, and the stone hand drags a little at the end of her arm, like a weight on a string. But she gets her feet under her, and her back straight, and she looks at him across the three paces of golden grass with the level, narrowed, merciless look that has frightened a great many generals.

"Lin Jian," she says. "I have been angry with you for a year."

"I know."

"A year of the Orchard. I sat under that tree and I was angry. I was angry at the Print and the secrets and the way you decide things alone and then ask us to bear them." Her voice is steady. "I was angry that you promised to tell me first and didn't. I was angry that you carried something that you were afraid I would see."

"Yue—"

"I was angry that I was afraid for you." She almost smiles. "Do you know how tiring that is?"

He says nothing.

"I'm done," says Yue.

"Done?"

"With the anger." She spreads her hands, the warm one and the cold. "It was a great deal of work. I don't think it did either of us any good. I think I'd rather be useful."

His eyes are very bright.

"I still can't tell you," he says. "Not all of it. Not yet."

"I know."

"I don't—it isn't that I don't trust you. It's that it's not mine to say. It was given to me, a long time ago, on terms I can't undo. If I told you, I'd lose it." He swallows. "And I can't lose it. Not until the end."

"What end?"

"The Door."

She studies him.

She has known this man for a long time. She has watched him lie, and watched him not lie, and learned to tell the difference by the set of the shoulders, the pitch of the voice, the way his good hand moves to his sleeve. He is not lying now. He is doing something harder. He is telling her the exact size of the thing he cannot tell her.

"All right," she says.

"All right?"

"I can work with that." She leans back against the bench and lets the stone hand rest on her knee. "You'll tell me when you can. I'll ask when I must. And in between, I'm going to be the person who stands next to you, and doesn't ask, and carries the water."

"Pebble carries the water."

"Pebble is asleep." A small, dry smile. "I'll carry it until he wakes."

---

Pebble wakes at the second Orchard hour, in a transport of apology.

He sits bolt upright on the bench with his eyes wide and his shaven head damp with sweat, and for a moment he cannot speak. Then he falls to his knees on the grass and bows, forehead to the ground, and says, in a voice thin with panic, that he has been sleeping, that it was unforgivable, that he should have kept watch, that the Master had told him to carry the water.

"Get up," says Yue.

"Master—"

"Pebble."

He gets up. He stands with his hands knotted and his chin trembling, a lean boy of seventeen in a tunic two sizes too large. Something in him has changed. It is not the height; he is the same. It is not the shoulders. It is something about the eyes, a quiet, bruised steadiness, like the surface of a well after the stone has gone down.

"You're Core," Jian says, gently.

Pebble blinks.

"I can see it. Hua can see it." He tilts his head. "You've done in a year what you'd have taken twenty to do. You're Core, Pebble. A clean one."

"I—" The boy looks at his hands. "I didn't feel anything."

"You wouldn't. It happens quietly." Jian smiles. It is a tired, kind, unguarded smile. "What did the tree ask you?"

"It asked what I was for."

"And?"

Pebble's mouth works.

"I said I was for staying," he says at last, very low. "I said it didn't matter what I was. That somebody had to be the one who stayed." He swallows. "And it said that was the best answer it had heard in six hundred years."

Nobody says anything.

Yue, watching the boy's face, feels a tightness in her chest that she does not examine. She reaches out with her right hand, the warm one, and puts it on his shoulder, and he flinches, and then leans into it, just slightly, as a plant leans to the sun.

"I told you you'd be useful," she says.

"You didn't."

"I thought it."

He laughs. It is a high, startled, cracked sound, and it is the first time she has heard it since the war.

---

She finds the pebble in her sleeve an hour later.

She has been sitting on the edge of the bench, with the stone hand lying in her lap, trying to teach it to hold a cup. It is not going well. The fingers close, and the cup is there, she can see it, she can feel the rim against her palm; but there is no warmth in the clay, no heat from the tea, and the first time she raises it to her mouth she tilts it too far and spills the whole thing down her front.

"You'll learn," says Hua, from the next bench, without opening her eyes.

"I know."

"It took Veyra a decade to get used to the key."

"I'm not Veyra."

"No." Hua's voice is dry. "You're a great deal less polite."

Yue snorts. She sets down the cup, and in the sleeve of her left arm, near the elbow, her fingers close on something small and flat and hard. She draws it out.

It is a gray river pebble, no bigger than a plum stone, smooth as glass. She had forgotten it. It lies in her stone palm, and she can see it, and she can feel its weight, a faint dull pressure, a tendon's report of a thing held. She cannot feel its warmth. It has been in her sleeve for forty-five years, against her skin, and it has taken on none of her heat.

You can give it back when you come home.

Yue closes her hand around it.

There is a small silence. The trees tick. Hua, on the next bench, has opened one eye.

"Little Mei," Yue says.

"The nursery girl."

"She's an old woman now. If she's alive. She'll be fifty-two." She hears her own voice go flat. "I told her I'd bring it back."

"You will."

"Will I?"

Hua's other eye opens. She pushes herself up on her elbow and looks at Yue, with her tired, clever, narrow face, and for a moment there is no Warden in it, only a girl, a plain girl of twenty-one who has lost a good deal and expects to lose more.

"I don't know," she says. "But I think the only way to find out is to keep climbing."

Yue nods, once.

She puts the pebble back in her sleeve.

---

The talk turns, after, to the world.

It begins with Jian asking a simple question: what was the state of things when she left? Yue answers it plainly. She tells him about the Hall of Ten Thousand Names, and the Roll, and the three thousand now woken; about Kuang's last scroll, and Hai Ren taking over the registry, and Tian Mo's forty men on the lower gate. She tells him about Little Mei and the white streak in Mei's hair. She tells him about the Sect's embassy, and Chao Wen's stiff promise, and the girl called Lan Xiu who walked down the Hundred Stairs with a child.

"She went to the Wall," Yue says. "They both did. The child's with Wenyuan."

Jian goes very still.

"With Wenyuan."

"You didn't know?"

"I knew she'd gone down. I didn't know where." He rubs his face with his steady hand. "She was carrying the white bell."

"Yes."

"And?"

Yue hesitates.

"I had a message by courier before I left," she says. "From Han. It said the Seam attacked. It said the tower held. It said—" She stops. "It said the Keystone sang."

"Sang what?"

"The Cradle."

Hua lets out a slow breath.

"He's blind now," Yue says. "That was the cost. Han didn't say it. But the courier did. He said the Keystone's eyes went dark, and a child sleeps at his feet, and a woman hums."

Jian's face is white.

"Qinghe," he says.

"I think so."

Nobody speaks.

After a moment, Veyra, from the edge of the grass, says in her cool flat voice: Then the Wall is held.

"For now," says Yue.

For now is all that anyone has. The hood tilts. I should know.

---

Sorrel finds them at dusk, which is a thing the Orchard does not have.

It is a trick of the light, she explains, as she crosses the grass with her basket on her arm. The honey fades to amber, the amber to bronze, and the trees lengthen their shadows in a long slow ritual that the Keeper calls the going-down. It is no more than a courtesy. Nothing in the Orchard really sets. But it gives the sitters a sense of days, and a person without days, she says, is a person who forgets to eat.

She sets down the basket and begins to unpack it.

There is bread, and cheese, and a jar of something sticky and sweet. There is a flask of tea, which Hua receives with a sound like a prayer. There are six small cups, and a little brass kettle, and an ingenious folding stool that Sorrel produces from the bottom of the basket with the air of a conjuror. The six of them, Jian and Yue and Hua and Pebble, with Veyra silent at the edge of the circle and the Keeper presiding, sit down on the grass in the going-down light and eat.

No one speaks for a long time.

It is Hua who breaks it.

"What now?" she says. She has a cup of tea cradled between both hands and a sliver of cheese on her knee. "I mean—the second year. Is it the same? Do we sit again?"

"You sit again," says Sorrel.

"For another forty-five years."

"For thirty-five, give or take. The seed is the hard part. The soul is only patience." The Keeper pours the tea. "But you needn't all go at once. The Row is long. I have forty trees at your disposal and a very great quantity of time. You might take the Nascent Soul in stages. A month. A week. A day." Her green eyes twinkle. "The Orchard is not a prison. It is a river. You may step out of it any time you like."

"And the world below?" says Jian.

"Goes on." The old woman shrugs. "It always does."

"How fast?"

"Forty to one." Sorrel stirs her tea. "And I should tell you, dears, that the Terraces above this one run faster. The Sixth is sixty to one. The Seventh, eighty. The Eighth—" She waves a hand. "You will see."

Jian is silent.

Yue watches him. She can see the arithmetic going on behind his eyes, the cold, careful, devastating sum: a year and a half to the Seventh Door, at eighty to one; ninety years outside; the Wall grown old; the Hall of Ten Thousand Names grown quiet; the people he loved gone to dust. She knows what it costs him. She has known it since the day he left.

"I can carry it," she says.

He looks up.

"The weight. The knowing." She holds his gaze. "I'm not asking you to share it. I'm saying I can bear it, if you need someone to. That's all."

His eyes are very bright. For a moment she thinks he will speak.

She is about to answer when she notices that the tea in her cup has stopped steaming, that the trees have stopped ticking, and that every one of the others has gone quiet in the same instant, like birds before a storm. Pebble's hand has found the hilt of the sword he does not carry. Veyra has turned her whole body toward the gate.

Then a long soft shadow falls across the grass, and the going-down light goes out like a snuffed lamp, and from the open gate at the end of the Row, a voice she has heard once before, on the Wall, a dry cool voice with a rasp in it like paper, says clearly:

"Good evening, Madam Yue. I am so glad you could join us."

Yue turns.

In the gate, tall and slender and hooded, with a ring of ember light on the back of his hand, stands the shadow of the Tenth.
